parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by nuclear binding energy.

markscheme_points.text: energy required to separate the nucleons (in the nucleus)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what holds a nucleus together. If the nucleons are bound, what would you have to do to get them completely apart from each other?
Hint 2: For full marks you need to say where the nucleons end up after separation - how far apart must they be so they no longer attract each other?
parts.proper_answer: The energy required to separate all the nucleons in a nucleus to infinity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What binding really means**
Think of a nucleus as tightly glued together by the strong nuclear force. The separate protons and neutrons have more mass-energy than when they are bound together. To break that glue you must put energy in.

Step 2: **Complete definition**
So binding energy is the minimum external energy you must supply to pull every proton and neutron completely apart so they no longer interact. In physics we say to infinite separation: $$ \text{binding energy = energy needed to separate all nucleons to infinity} $$

parts.label: (a)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: curve starting close to the origin and forming a single peak
peak shown to left of centre, with steep line on LHS of peak and shallow

hints: Hint 1: Recall the famous shape - it starts very low for light nuclei like H and He, then climbs very quickly. Where is the most stable nucleus on the A axis?
Hint 2: After the peak, what happens for heavy nuclei up to A = 250? Think steep rise on the left, broad maximum around A = 50 to 60, then gentle fall to the right.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starts near origin at low E, rises steeply to a single broad maximum at A about 50-60, then falls slowly and gradually toward A = 250.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember the shape**
Binding energy per nucleon $E$ tells you stability per particle. Very light nuclei have low $E$. As $A$ increases, $E$ shoots up steeply because adding nucleons adds a lot of strong-force attraction.

Step 2: **Peak and tail**
The curve reaches a single peak around iron, $A \approx 56$, the most stable nucleus. For heavier nuclei the extra protons add Coulomb repulsion, so $E$ slowly decreases: $$ \text{steep rise from origin} \rightarrow \text{peak left of centre} \rightarrow \text{slow fall to } A=250 $$ Start your line close to the origin, not at zero, and do not draw multiple peaks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
In one type of nuclear process, deuterium ($^{2}_{1}\text{H}$) undergoes the reaction
$$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{2}_{1}\text{H} \longrightarrow ^{3}_{2}\text{He} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n}.$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State the name of this type of nuclear process.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the reaction: two very light $^{2}_{1}$H nuclei join to make a heavier $^{3}_{2}$He. Are small nuclei splitting apart or joining together?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot joining vs splitting**
Here two deuterium nuclei, each with $A=2$, combine to form a larger nucleus with $A=3$ plus a neutron. Light nuclei joining to form a heavier nucleus is fusion, the process that powers stars.

enrichment.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the reaction: two very light $^{2}_{1}$H nuclei join to make a heavier $^{3}_{2}$He. Are small nuclei splitting apart or joining together?

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain, with reference to your line in (a)(ii), why this reaction results in the release of energy.

markscheme_points.text: both particles have low A values or both particles are at left-hand end of graph
He-3 has higher binding energy (per nucleon) than H-2

hints: Hint 1: Locate both nuclei on your curve from (a)(ii). Both $^{2}$H and $^{3}$He have very small A, so which region of the graph are they in?
Hint 2: Compare their heights on the graph. If the product has a larger E than the reactant, what does that increase in binding mean for released energy?
parts.proper_answer: Both nuclei are light nuclei at the left-hand end of the curve. $^{3}$He has greater binding energy per nucleon than $^{2}$H, so total binding energy increases and the difference is released as energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the left side of the curve**
Both $^{2}$H ($A=2$) and $^{3}$He ($A=3$) sit on the steep rising part on the far left. Moving to larger $A$ there means moving uphill to higher $E$.

Step 2: **Link higher E to release**
$^{3}$He is more tightly bound per nucleon than $^{2}$H. Total binding energy after is greater than before. The extra binding comes from a loss of mass, which appears as kinetic energy and radiation: $$ E_{product} > E_{reactant} \text{ so energy is released} $$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Table 8.1 shows the masses of the particles involved in the reaction in (b).
Table 8.1
| particle | mass / $\text{u}$ |
| $^{1}_{0}\text{n}$ | 1.008665 |
| $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ | 2.014102 |
| $^{3}_{2}\text{He}$ | 3.016029 |
Calculate the energy released when $1.00\text{ mol}$ of deuterium undergoes the reaction.

markscheme_points.text: 1.00 mol of deuterium forms 0.500 mol of helium-3

hints: Hint 1: Start with mass balance. How does total mass before (two deuterium nuclei) compare with total mass after (helium-3 plus neutron)?
Hint 2: Recall $E = \Delta m c^{2}$ but $\Delta m$ is in u. What conversion do you need to get mass in kg before using $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8} \text{ m s}^{-1}$?
Hint 3: That energy is for one single reaction using two deuterium nuclei. If you have 1.00 mol of deuterium, how many reactions can actually occur?
Hint 4: Now scale up: multiply the number of reactions by Avogadro number $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ and by the energy per reaction to get total energy in J.
Hint 5: Check your powers of ten carefully: $1 \text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ and remember to halve the moles because two deuterium are needed per reaction.
parts.proper_answer: Mass defect per reaction $\approx 0.00351 \text{ u}$, energy per reaction $\approx 5.24 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$, total energy for 1.00 mol deuterium $\approx 1.58 \times 10^{11} \text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the mass defect**
Mass before minus mass after gives the mass lost: $$ \Delta m = [2 \times m(^{2}_{1}\text{H}) - m(^{3}_{2}\text{He}) - m(^{1}_{0}\text{n})] $$ $$ \Delta m = [(2 \times 2.014102) - (3.016029 + 1.008665)]\text{ u} = 0.00351\text{ u} $$ Positive means mass is lost.

Step 2: **Convert to energy for one reaction**
Use Einstein relation $E = \Delta m c^{2}$. First convert u to kg with $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$: $$ E = 0.00351 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \times (3.00 \times 10^{8})^{2} $$ $$ E \approx 5.24 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J} $$ This is the energy released by one fusion event.

Step 3: **Scale from one nucleus to one mole**
Each reaction needs 2 deuterium nuclei, so 1.00 mol of deuterium makes only 0.500 mol of reactions. Number of reactions is: $$ N = 0.500 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} $$ Total energy: $$ E_{total} = N \times 5.24 \times 10^{-13} \approx 1.58 \times 10^{11}\text{ J} $$ A common mistake is to forget the factor of 0.5 and overestimate by two times.
